content: When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles. {{v:15}} He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer, {{v:16}} for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in God’s Kingdom.” {{v:17}} He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this and share it among yourselves, {{v:18}} for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God’s Kingdom comes.” {{v:19}} He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.” {{v:20}} Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you. {{v:21}} But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. {{v:22}} The Son of Man indeed goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!” {{v:23}} They began to question among themselves which of them it was who would do this thing.

facets.text: Jesus institutes the Eucharist within the Passover meal, identifying the bread as his body "given for you" and the cup as "the new covenant in my blood." By locating the sacrament in the Passover context, Luke presents Christ as the true Paschal Lamb whose sacrifice delivers God's people, fulfilling and surpassing the exodus deliverance. The Eucharist is thus the memorial of the new and definitive Passover.
facets.question: How does the Eucharist fulfill and transform the Passover?

facets.text: The words "This is my body" and "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" express the real gift of Christ himself under the signs of bread and wine. The language is not merely symbolic but covenantal and sacrificial, echoing the blood of the covenant at Sinai now surpassed by the blood "poured out for you." Catholic faith reads these words as establishing the Real Presence and the sacrifice made present in the Mass.
facets.question: What do Jesus's words over the bread and cup reveal about his real presence?

facets.text: Christ's command, "Do this in memory of me," institutes the Eucharist as an ongoing memorial and confers on the apostles the office of celebrating it. This is not mere recollection but an anamnesis that makes the one sacrifice of the cross truly present. In these words the tradition sees the foundation of the ministerial priesthood and the perpetual offering of the Mass.
facets.question: What does it mean that Jesus commanded the apostles to celebrate the Eucharist in his memory?

facets.text: Jesus twice speaks of not eating or drinking again "until God's Kingdom comes," giving the Supper an eschatological orientation. The Eucharist looks forward to the messianic banquet and the consummation of the Kingdom, so that every celebration is both a memorial of the cross and a pledge of future glory. The meal binds Christ's Passion to the promise of eternal communion with him in the Kingdom.
facets.question: How does the Last Supper point toward the coming Kingdom of God?

facets.text: Jesus reveals that his betrayer shares the table with him, yet affirms that "the Son of Man indeed goes as it has been determined." Divine providence embraces even the treachery of the betrayal, weaving human sin into the accomplishment of salvation, while the solemn "woe" preserves the betrayer's full moral responsibility. Predestined purpose and free human guilt stand together without contradiction.
facets.question: How can Jesus's betrayal be both foreordained and the betrayer's own guilt?

facets.text: Jesus declares he has "earnestly desired to eat this Passover" before he suffers, disclosing the depth of his loving intention toward his own on the eve of his Passion. The gift of the Eucharist flows from this ardent desire, revealing that his self-offering is willed with love rather than merely endured. The Supper is the expression of a heart that longs to give itself for the disciples.
facets.question: Why did Jesus earnestly desire to share this Passover before his suffering?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: At the Last Supper Luke recounts Jesus's institution of the Eucharist within the Passover, his covenantal words over bread and cup, the command to continue the memorial, its eschatological horizon, and the announcement of the betrayer. Scope spans Eucharistic theology, sacrifice, priesthood, providence, and Christ's loving intent.

[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Jesus as the true Paschal Lamb institutes the Eucharist within Passover, fulfilling and surpassing the exodus deliverance in a new Passover.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The words over bread and cup establish Christ's real presence and the sacrificial new covenant in his blood poured out.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: "Do this in memory of me" institutes the Eucharist as anamnesis and grounds the ministerial priesthood and the perpetual offering of the Mass.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The repeated "until God's Kingdom comes" gives the Supper an eschatological orientation toward the messianic banquet and future glory.
[PHILOSOPHICAL | inferential]: The betrayal is foreordained yet freely guilty; divine providence embraces human sin without removing the betrayer's moral responsibility.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: Jesus's "earnest desire" to eat this Passover reveals the loving intention behind his self-offering in the Eucharist.
